tagline: A Blue Ridge crest road with mileposts counting south from Front Royal.
intro: Skyline Drive winds for 105 miles along the Blue Ridge crest through Shenandoah National Park. Its two lanes connect 75 overlooks facing the Shenandoah Valley to the west and the Piedmont to the east. Designated a National Scenic Byway in 2005, it is the park’s only public through road. The National Park Service describes a crest-top drive taking about three hours on a clear day, with a 35 mph limit in most places.

The 1924 proposal for the park made a road with valley and Piedmont views its central feature. President Herbert Hoover called for construction in 1929, and groundbreaking followed in 1931. The first section opened in 1934; Civilian Conservation Corps workers built overlooks and stone walls and planted trees and shrubs. Early road funding employed local farmers and apple pickers who had suffered through the severe drought of 1930. Creating the park and road also displaced residents, some forcibly, and homes were demolished.

Travel south from Front Royal to Thornton Gap, then through Marys Rock Tunnel toward Skyland and the Hawksbill trailheads. Big Meadows lies near the middle at mile 51. Continue through Swift Run Gap to Rockfish Gap, where Skyline Drive meets the Blue Ridge Parkway. Cement mileposts on the road’s west side mark the journey from 0 to 105.

moments.title: Marys Rock Tunnel
moments.text: Marys Rock Tunnel takes Skyline Drive through the mountain at mile 32.2. The two-lane passage is 670 feet long. Engineers chose a tunnel instead of an open cut; the road history records cost saving as its justification. In 1958, part of the tunnel received a concrete lining to prevent winter icicles and summer water seepage. The National Park Service gives a maximum clearance of 12 feet 8 inches, measured for both lanes. It is the only vehicle tunnel in Shenandoah National Park. Its two lanes carry the park road beneath the east slopes of Marys Rock.

moments.title: Skyland
moments.text: Skyland was built as Stony Man Camp in 1895; its early guests arrived by horse or wagon. George Freeman Pollock built the resort on land his father largely owned, intending it for affluent visitors from major cities. It even advertised itself as a dude ranch. Skyline Drive later passed the resort at the road’s highest point, 3,680 feet. The park expanded Skyland’s accommodations while removing older improvements in much of the surrounding park. The view here reaches across the Shenandoah Valley, and the expanded accommodations remain available to visitors at the old resort site.

moments.title: Hawksbill Mountain
moments.text: Balsam fir grows at Hawksbill’s summit, one of the few places in Shenandoah National Park where this northern tree occurs. Hawksbill is the park’s highest point, with a north face dropping 2,500 feet into Timber Hollow. A short hike from Upper Hawksbill parking leads to the summit, where the National Park Service built a stone observation platform. The Appalachian Trail passes below the top rather than crossing it. The summit marks the boundary between Madison and Page counties. Its firs are more typical of northern New England and southeastern Canada.

moments.title: Big Meadows
moments.text: At mile 51, Big Meadows is the park’s largest developed area. The meadow lies beside the visitor center and camp store, with grassy paths across it. Nearby, a trail descends to Dark Hollow Falls, a 70-foot waterfall. The waterfall trail is 0.7 mile from its parking lot and steep on the return.

practical: Marys Rock Tunnel: Marys Rock Tunnel clearance is 12 feet 8 inches in both lanes. Weather can close Skyline Drive at any time; consult park alerts before driving. (checked 2026-10-11)
